title: Realtime Database
objectives: Understand Realtime Database via a real-life analogy
Structure data as a shallow JSON tree
Implement presence + low-latency sync via onDisconnect()

sections.markdown:
**Think of Realtime Database as a shared Google Doc that's also a JSON tree.**

Everyone who opens the doc sees the SAME live text. If Alice types 'hello' — Bob sees 'hello' appear letter-by-letter in real time. No refresh, no polling — a persistent WebSocket streams changes.

RTDB is that, but for structured data. **The entire database is ONE giant JSON object**, rooted at `/`. Every path (`/rooms/xyz/messages`) is a node in the tree. You can:
- **Read** the value at any path.
- **Listen** to a path — get pushed every change, forever, in ~10ms.
- **Write** at any path — all connected listeners see the update instantly.
- **`onDisconnect()`** — schedule writes to happen when a client's WebSocket drops (network dies, phone locked, app killed). Perfect for **presence**: 'set `/users/me/status = offline` when I disconnect.'

**This is Firebase's ORIGINAL database (2012).** Rock-solid; the runtime engine behind chats, live games, presence, collaborative whiteboards for years.

**But — the model has costs:**
- **Single JSON tree** = no complex queries. `orderByChild` is the closest thing to indexing. No composite queries. No joins.
- **Read charges by DATA VOLUME**, not doc count. Reading a large subtree = paying for all of it.
- **Deep nesting is dangerous** — reading a parent reads everything below it, unless you `shallow()` (limited).
- **Single-shard scaling** — one RTDB instance handles ~200K concurrent users before needing manual sharding.

**Firestore** (2017) fixed these — collections + documents, composite queries, per-doc reads, multi-region. **For most new apps, Firestore is the default.** RTDB is best when you specifically need: **ultra-low-latency (< 20ms) presence + sync**, existing RTDB codebases, or genuinely simple KV-tree data.

**Interview take:** Know when to reach for RTDB (chat presence, live games, whiteboards) vs Firestore (everything else). This is a classic 'senior engineer' architecture question.

**Realtime Database (RTDB)** is Firebase's original database — a JSON tree store synchronized in real time via a persistent WebSocket. Reads/writes stream to all listeners within milliseconds. **Storage model:** one giant JSON object at `/`; every path is a node. **Cost model:** by data VOLUME (GB downloaded, GB stored), not doc count. **Superpowers:** presence via `onDisconnect()`, ultra-low-latency sync, simple KV/tree API. **Weaknesses:** limited queries (single `orderByChild`), single-shard scaling, download costs on deep reads. **Prefer Firestore for new apps** unless you specifically need RTDB's presence or ultra-low latency.

## RTDB vs Firestore — the decision matrix
**Rule of thumb:** New app → Firestore. Existing RTDB codebase → stay unless you have a reason to migrate. Chat + presence-heavy → RTDB is still competitive.
## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Deep nesting.** Reading a top-level node reads GB of data. Flatten to shallow structure.
**Mistake 2: Loading whole subtree for a list view.** Query with `limitToLast(N)`; don't fetch all messages ever.
**Mistake 3: Cascading rules.** If parent has `.read: true`, ALL children are readable — even if a child rule says false. Rules are additive downward.
**Mistake 4: No presence disconnect handler.** User closes app → shows online forever. Always `onDisconnect().set('offline')`.
**Mistake 5: Client-generated timestamps.** Devices lie. Use `ServerValue.timestamp`.
**Mistake 6: Not using `orderByChild` indexes.** Query without an index rule → full-tree scan. Add `.indexOn` in rules.
**Mistake 7: Single-instance overload.** RTDB scales to ~200K concurrent per instance. Beyond that, shard manually.
## Best practices
**1. Flatten the tree.** `users/`, `rooms/`, `messages/` at top level, not deeply nested.
**2. Always `limit()` queries.** Never fetch unbounded lists.
**3. `onDisconnect()` for presence.** Non-negotiable for online status.
**4. `ServerValue.timestamp` for all times.** Immune to device clock drift.
**5. `.indexOn` for query paths.** Rules with `.indexOn: ['ts', 'from']` enable server-side indexes.
**6. Offline persistence on.** `setPersistenceEnabled(true)` at init.
**7. Design for the worst reader.** If a rule grants read at level N, everything below is exposed. Structure paths intentionally.
**8. For big apps, plan sharding early.** Multiple RTDB instances if traffic > 200K concurrent.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy) — Chat room.** `rooms/{id}/messages` — push + limit to last 50 — real-time list.
**Practice 2 (Medium) — Presence.** `onDisconnect().set('offline')` + `set('online')`. Test by killing app; verify status updates.
**Practice 3 (Medium) — Rules with indexOn.** Query `messages` by `ts`; add `.indexOn` rule; verify no warning.
**Practice 4 (Hard) — Flatten a nested tree.** Take `users/{uid}/friends/{fid}/messages/...` (5 levels) → flatten to `messages/{msgId}` with denormalized fields; measure read savings.
**Practice 5 (Hard) — Optimistic transaction.** Multi-user counter increment via `runTransaction`; observe automatic retries.
**Practice 6 (Expert) — Shard across instances.** Route `us-users` to instance A, `eu-users` to B; unified rules.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: RTDB vs Firestore — when to use each?**

**A:** **RTDB (Realtime Database)** — single JSON tree, ultra-low-latency (~10-50ms) sync via WebSocket, **presence via `onDisconnect()`**, simple queries only. Cost per GB stored + downloaded. Superpowers: chat, presence, live games, whiteboards. Scaling limit: ~200K concurrent per instance. **Firestore** — collections of documents, composite queries, multi-region auto-scaling, per-doc read cost. Better for: everything else — CRUD apps, complex queries, multi-tenant. **My rule for new apps:** default to Firestore. Reach for RTDB when you specifically need **presence** or **ultra-low latency**. Some apps use BOTH — Firestore for main data, RTDB for presence + typing indicators. Real-world: WhatsApp-like chat pairs RTDB (typing/presence) with Firestore (message store). **This is THE classic Firebase-architect interview question.**

**Q2: How does presence work with `onDisconnect()`?**

**A:** The client SCHEDULES a write to happen when its WebSocket connection dies — the server, not the client, executes it. **Flow:** (1) Client connects, sends `ref.onDisconnect().set('offline')` — server records the intent. (2) Client sends `ref.set('online')` — status is now online. (3) Client's WebSocket closes (app killed, network drops, phone locks) — server detects within seconds and executes the scheduled offline write. **Why this matters:** naive presence based on client-sent 'goodbye' messages FAILS on network drops. `onDisconnect` runs on the server, so it's reliable. **Combined pattern:** last-seen timestamp — `onDisconnect().update({status: 'offline', lastSeen: ServerValue.timestamp})`. **Firestore doesn't have this** — it's RTDB's killer feature. Every chat/social app that shows online status uses this. **Interview take:** 'This is why presence at scale is easier in RTDB than Firestore.'

**Q3: How do RTDB Security Rules differ from Firestore's?**

**A:** **Format:** RTDB rules are JSON with `.read`, `.write`, `.validate`, `.indexOn` at each node. Firestore rules are a JS-like DSL with `match /path { allow read: if ... }`. **Semantics — the key difference:** RTDB rules **cascade downward**. Grant `.read: true` at `/users` → EVERY child under `/users` is readable, no way to un-grant. Firestore rules are per-path, non-cascading. **Consequence:** RTDB path design is critical — put private data at separate top-level paths from public. **Built-ins:** RTDB has `auth`, `data`, `newData`, `root`, `$wildcard`. Firestore has `request.auth`, `resource`, `request.resource`. **Validation:** RTDB has a dedicated `.validate` per node. Firestore mixes it into `allow write`. **Default:** both deny. **Interview take:** cascading rules trip up newcomers — 'why can they read this? I set the child rule to false.' The answer: the parent granted it.

**Q4: How do you avoid huge reads in RTDB?**

**A:** Two levers: **(1) Flatten the tree.** Instead of `users/{uid}/rooms/{rid}/messages/{msgId}` (5 levels; reading a user pulls ALL their message history), separate: `users/{uid}`, `rooms/{rid}`, `messages/{msgId}` at top level with foreign-key references. **(2) Query with limits.** Always `limitToLast(50)` or `limitToFirst(20)` — never fetch unbounded lists. **(3) `orderByChild + startAt/endAt`** for pagination. **(4) `shallow` reads (REST API only)** — get just direct children, not deep tree. **(5) Split hot subtrees** — `messages/{msgId}` (metadata) vs `messages/{msgId}/attachments/` (heavy). **Detection:** Firebase console → RTDB usage → bandwidth chart. Spikes = someone loaded a big subtree. **Add `.indexOn` on `orderByChild` fields** — otherwise queries scan the whole subtree, which is a performance AND cost disaster. Every scaled RTDB app fights this fight.

**Q5: What's RTDB's scaling model?**

**A:** Each RTDB **instance** is a single Firebase Realtime Database URL (e.g., `my-app.firebaseio.com`). **One instance handles ~200,000 concurrent connections and ~1000 write ops/sec** — Google-provided soft limits. Beyond that: **manual sharding**. Provision additional RTDB instances (e.g., `my-app-shard-2.firebaseio.com`) and route traffic based on region, tenant, or user hash. Different instances can't cross-query — sharding pushes complexity to your app layer. **Storage limit:** 1 GB free, up to 1 TB per instance. **Compare Firestore:** automatic multi-region scaling; no manual sharding needed; single global project handles millions of concurrent. **This is a common answer to 'why did team X migrate off RTDB' — hit the shard wall.** For most apps, one instance suffices. Interview take: 'Plan sharding early only if you're building the next WhatsApp; for typical apps, one instance is enough.'

**Q6: What are common RTDB cost drivers and fixes?**

**A:** RTDB bills for **GB stored + GB downloaded** — not per-op like Firestore. **Big cost drivers:** (1) **Deep-tree reads** — one careless `ref('/users').once()` downloads ALL users. Fix: shallow reads or narrow paths. (2) **Real-time listener bandwidth** — a listener that fires 1000×/day per user × 1M users = petabytes. Cache with `keepSynced(true)` for hot paths; SDK avoids redundant fetches. (3) **No client-side offline persistence** — every read hits network. `setPersistenceEnabled(true)` is free perf + cost win. (4) **Unlimited pagination** — `limitToLast(50)` religiously. (5) **Zombie listeners** — a Widget that leaks its `onValue` subscription keeps consuming bandwidth. Dispose. (6) **Big documents** — RTDB doesn't page fields; if a message has a 500KB image blob, every fetch of the message pulls it. Store blob in Cloud Storage; put URL in RTDB. **Monitor:** Firebase console → RTDB → Bandwidth chart. Look for anomalous spikes.

## Real-world usage

- **Chat + collaborative apps** — presence is RTDB's killer feature.
- **Live games** — leaderboards, multiplayer state.
- **Whiteboards / collaborative docs** — tiny writes broadcast to peers instantly.
- **IoT + telemetry** — high-frequency small writes.
- **NOT for** — complex queries, deep multi-tenant hierarchies, analytics.

## Advanced notes

- **Multi-database projects** — 1 project can host multiple RTDB instances; specify URL when initializing.
- **`.indexOn`** rule — must add for `orderByChild` paths to avoid full-tree scans.
- **`keepSynced(true)`** — pre-cache a path; keeps it up-to-date offline.
- **REST API** — for backend without full SDK; supports `shallow=true` for lightweight reads.
- **Cloud Functions triggers** — `onWrite`, `onCreate`, `onUpdate`, `onDelete` on any path.
- **BigQuery streaming import** — no built-in; must wire manually via Cloud Function.
- **Emulator** — `firebase emulators:start --only database`.
- **Data model migration** — RTDB → Firestore is common; scripts + `admin.database().ref().once()` to export.
- **Backup** — manual export via REST API or `gcloud firebase database` CLI.
- **Compaction** — automatic; you don't manage GC.
- **onDisconnect chained** — set multiple paths + cancel operations.
- **Priority + orderByPriority** — legacy; prefer `orderByChild`.
- **Encryption** — encrypted at rest; TLS in transit.
- **Compliance** — HIPAA / GDPR require BAA + config; talk to Google Cloud sales.
